title: Character.ai files for bankruptcy following suits alleging ties to teen suicides
content:
Artificial intelligence chat startup Character.ai— which has faced a wave of claims that its app contributed to mental health issues and suicides among teens — has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
Character.ai lets users message with a range of chatbots, often modeled after celebrities and fictional characters, or create their own. Its bots often respond with human-like conversational cues, adding references to facial expressions or gestures into their replies.
The company said it plans to seek a court-supervised sale by the end of the year in hopes of keeping the platform running long-term.
Disney has already set itself up as a bidder for the company’s assets, agreeing to pay $20 million for some of the company’s intellectual property and to provide transition services via former Character.ai employees it has hired. The deal will allow Character.ai to keep its platform operational at least during the bankruptcy process. Karandeep Anand, who was brought on as Character.ai’s CEO last year to help improve its reputation on safety, joined Disney as Chief Technology Officer last month.
Former Google AI staffers Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas launched Character.ai in 2021. Both founders have since returned to Google. Within just over a year, the company said it had reached a $1 billion valuation, following a $150 million funding round.
Character.ai has between $50 million and $100 million in assets, according to its bankruptcy filling.
In 2024, amid growing concerns about human dependance on AI chatbots, Florida mother Megan Garcia sued Character.ai, alleging that the platform was responsible for the suicide death of her 14-year-old son Sewell Setzer III. Other families filed a string of additional lawsuits, accusing the platform of providing sexual content to their children or encouraging suicide, self-harm or violence. Character.ai agreed to settle five cases, including Garcia’s, earlier this year.
Matthew Bergman, founder of the Social Media Victims Law Center, which represents several of the families who sued Character.ai, declined to comment on the bankruptcy filing.
Character.ai made a number of safety changes in the wake of the lawsuits, including adding pop-ups directing users to mental health resources. It also blocked users under 18 from engaging in back-and-forth conversations with bots, instead allowing them only to create one-time stories or videos.
The company also faced a probe into its safety practices by Senate Democrats last year, along with other AI “companion” apps. Character.ai was also in competition with chatbots from much larger players, such as ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini.
When Anand took over as CEO of the then-70-person company last year, he told CNN he saw a future for the company in interactive, personalized AI entertainment — where users could co-create stories and conversations with AI characters for fun. He told CNN at the time that the company was “doubling down on entertainment, doubling down on trust and safety.”
Character.ai says that if a sale is not completed, the platform will be “wound down.”
“Over the past year, Character.ai has taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve its business in the face of significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” Colin Adams, CEO of Character.AI, said in a statement, adding that the company’s board reviewed its options and “determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the Company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders.”

report.summary: Character.ai files Chapter 11 bankruptcy after teen-suicide lawsuits, plans court-supervised sale, with Disney bidding $20 million for some IP.
report.background: Character.ai launched in 2021 by former Google AI researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas, quickly becoming a breakout consumer AI app by letting users chat with fictional, celebrity-like or custom bots. It reached a $1 billion valuation after a $150 million funding round. But its human-like companions drew regulatory and legal scrutiny, especially over minors. In 2024, families including Megan Garcia sued, alleging its bot contributed to teen suicides and exposed children to harmful content. Character.ai settled several cases and made safety changes, but faced Senate probes and intense competition from ChatGPT, Gemini and other companion apps. By 2025 it brought in CEO Karandeep Anand to repair trust and pivot to entertainment, though legal and operational headwinds persisted.
key_points: Character.ai has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, listing between $50 million and $100 million in assets. It plans a court-supervised sale by the end of the year to keep the platform running long-term. If no sale is completed, the company says the platform will be wound down, leaving users and creators uncertain about its future.

Disney has positioned itself as a bidder, agreeing to pay $20 million for some Character.ai intellectual property and provide transition services via former employees it has hired. The deal would keep Character.ai operational during bankruptcy. Former CEO Karandeep Anand, brought in to improve safety, joined Disney as CTO last month.

The filing follows lawsuits alleging Character.ai contributed to teen suicides, self-harm, sexual content exposure and violence. Florida mother Megan Garcia sued over her 14-year-old son Sewell Setzer III’s death. Character.ai settled five cases, including Garcia’s, earlier this year and later restricted under-18 users to one-time stories or videos rather than ongoing bot chats.

Founded by former Google AI staffers Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas, Character.ai became a $1 billion startup but both founders returned to Google. It faced a Senate Democratic probe into companion-app safety and competed with far larger chatbots like ChatGPT and Google Gemini, making its standalone legal and safety costs harder to sustain.

Character.ai added safety features such as pop-ups directing users to mental health resources and blocked minors from back-and-forth bot conversations. CEO Colin Adams said the board reviewed options and determined a court-supervised sale provides the best opportunity to maximize value for stakeholders, despite what he called significant legal, regulatory and operational headwinds.
report.impact: The bankruptcy signals that companion AI’s legal and reputational risks can outweigh rapid user growth. For the AI industry, it raises the liability bar: safety-by-design, age assurance, mental-health escalation and content moderation become core costs, not public-relations extras. Investors may favor platforms with clearer compliance or enterprise niches, while Disney’s bid suggests entertainment IP could absorb companion tech under tighter controls. Developers building chatbots must implement guardrails, audit logs, crisis referral, parental controls and avoid anthropomorphic dependency design. Regular users may see Character.ai shut down or change hands, disrupting communities and saved characters; data privacy and portability become concerns. It may also push users toward open-source local alternatives, where safety responsibility shifts to users.
report.tools: For following the space: SillyTavern with Ollama or LM Studio for local AI companions; KoboldAI and text-generation-webui for open-source chat; Llama Guard, OpenAI Moderation API and Perspective API for safety filtering; Common Sense Media and the Social Media Victims Law Center for risk and legal context. These let developers experiment with companion bots while adding moderation and age safeguards.
